lessons.title: Text Variables
intro: The first BASIC could only handle numbers. Later editions added text variables, also called strings. Their names end with a dollar sign: N$, A$, X1$.
LET N$ = "ADA" stores a word. PRINT N$ shows it, and INPUT N$ lets the user type a word or name.
Text and numbers are kept apart: N$ can't hold a number for calculating, and N can't hold text.

exercises.prompt: Which one is a text variable?
exercises.explanation: Text variables end with $. Some people read N$ as N-string.
The semicolons glue the three pieces together: GOOD, a space, and MORNING.

exercises.prompt: Store the word YES in W$.
exercises.explanation: Text in a program always needs double quotes. Without them, BASIC would think YES is a variable name.

exercises.prompt: This program stops with ?TYPE MISMATCH. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explanation: N is a number variable, so it can't hold text. It should be LET N$ = "BOB" and PRINT N$.

exercises.prompt: The user types MAX. What does this program print at the end?
exercises.explanation: N$ holds MAX, followed directly by the text " IS HERE", which starts with a space.

exercises.prompt: Build a program that asks for a color and repeats it.
exercises.explanation: Ask, read the word into a text variable, and print it back.

lessons.title: Text in Decisions and Data
intro: IF works with text too: IF A$ = "YES" THEN 100. Only exactly the same text counts as equal.
DATA lines can hold text in quotes, mixed with numbers. READ N$, A takes a name and then a number, in that order.
Text lists work like number lists: N$(1), N$(2) and so on. That's perfect for names, words or quiz questions.

exercises.prompt: What is in the second row of the example's output?
exercises.explanation: Each round reads one name and one year. The second round gets ALAN and 1912.

exercises.prompt: The user types NO. What does this program print?
exercises.explanation: NO isn't equal to YES, so the program doesn't jump and prints MAYBE LATER.

exercises.prompt: Store the second name in a text list.
exercises.explanation: The position in a text list is a number, just like in number lists.

exercises.prompt: This stops with ?TYPE MISMATCH. Which line has the values in the wrong order?
exercises.explanation: READ takes the values in order. The first value is the text ADA, but it should go into the number A. Either READ N$, A or swap the DATA.
Text is compared alphabetically, so ANNA comes before BEN. That's how lists of names can be sorted.

exercises.prompt: The user types Yes. Does IF A$ = "YES" THEN 100 jump?
options: No, the text must match exactly, including capital letters
exercises.explanation: Yes and YES are different texts. Old teletypes only had capital letters, so this rarely mattered back then.

lessons.title: Whole Lists with MAT
intro: Dartmouth BASIC was made for science students, who constantly work with tables of numbers called matrices. So BASIC got MAT statements that work on a whole list at once.
MAT READ A fills the entire list A from DATA, and MAT PRINT A prints all of it. MAT C = A + B adds two lists element by element. MAT always uses positions 1 up to the DIM size.
The real MAT could also handle two-dimensional tables and multiply matrices. Here we use it on simple lists.

exercises.prompt: After DIM A(4), how many values does MAT READ A read?
exercises.explanation: MAT works with positions 1 up to the DIM size, so it reads 4 values.

exercises.prompt: Fill the whole list A from the DATA line in one go.
exercises.explanation: MAT READ replaces a whole FOR loop with READ A(I) inside.

exercises.prompt: A holds 5, 5, 5 and B holds 1, 2, 3. What does MAT C = A - B give?
exercises.explanation: Each position is calculated on its own: 5 - 1, 5 - 2 and 5 - 3.

exercises.prompt: What does MAT PRINT A do?
options: It prints every value of the list in columns
It prints the size of the list
exercises.explanation: MAT PRINT goes through the whole list and lines the values up in print zones.

exercises.prompt: Why did Dartmouth BASIC have MAT statements?
options: Science and engineering students worked with tables of numbers all the time
Because FOR loops didn't exist yet
exercises.explanation: Matrices are everywhere in physics, engineering and statistics. MAT made that work quick to write.

exercises.prompt: This stops with ?MAT SIZES DON'T MATCH. Which line causes it?
exercises.explanation: A has 3 places and B has 4, so they can't be added element by element. Both need the same size.
